text: Cassini had spent years near Titan and Enceladus, so the spacecraft carried a small but real risk of Earth microorganisms hitching a ride. If its orbit degraded and it struck a moon, it could introduce contaminants into places that might host life. The Grand Finale solved this by steering it into Saturn’s atmosphere, where it disintegrates. A gas giant is a clean disposal site: no surface to leave debris or microbes behind. This was standard planetary protection practice. It also let Cassini gather high-resolution data on Saturn’s rings and polar regions before the final plunge at the end of its mission.

Hi Sam,

The stationary leg on a skateboard is doing an isometric hold in a half-flexed position. That means the quads and hip flexors are working hard just to keep your body balanced and stable while the other leg pushes. You're not moving that leg, but the muscles are contracting continuously, and that kind of sustained tension fatigues the fibers quickly. That's why you get a dull ache after a while. The hip flexors and adductors are also under sustained tension because your stance keeps the hip in a partially flexed posture.

The other thing is that you probably favor one leg as the pusher. That creates an imbalance where the non-pusher leg takes more load and becomes sore. I'd alternate which leg stays still, and I'd vary your pusher leg during a session. If you always push with the right leg, your left is the stationary one, and that's the one that ends up aching.

For the soreness itself, the muscles are likely tight from the sustained contraction. A stretch of the hip flexors and quads after riding helps. A lunge stretch for the hip flexor, a quad stretch by pulling the heel toward the glutes. If the pain is sharp or in the groin, check your adductors. If it's a deep ache in the front of the thigh, it's the quads and hip flexors.

Practical fixes: warm up before you ride. A couple of minutes of walking or light jogging gets blood into those muscles. Keep your knees bent slightly so you're not locking the joint. If you're riding on rough ground, the stationary leg absorbs more impact, which adds to the strain.

If your stance is too wide or your weight is too far back, the stationary leg has to work harder to keep you upright. Move your weight forward a bit and keep your shoulders square. That reduces the isometric load on the hip and thigh.

If it keeps hurting, try not pushing so hard and keep the ride shorter until the legs adapt. The muscles build tolerance over a few sessions.

— Sam

The name does not mean the person currently lives in Africa. It means they are of African descent. Most Black Americans have ancestors who came from West and Central Africa, often as enslaved people, so the African part refers to ancestry, not residence. A person born in Detroit or Atlanta is still considered African American if their family line comes from Africa. The term describes heritage, not citizenship or immigration status. Some are first-generation immigrants, and others are descendants of enslaved Africans. Both groups share the same broad identity. In everyday US usage, African American is the standard form; Afro-American is less common and sounds older. Preferences vary by individual, so some people say Black American and avoid the Africa reference. If someone uses Afro-American, they are not claiming the person was born on the continent. The label points to the African side of ancestral identity, not to birthplace. The hyphenated form appears more in mid-century writing and older textbooks. For many people, the term is an ethnic label, like Italian-American or German-American. It groups people by descent from the African continent, not by present location. That distinction matters for identity debates.

Syrians get weapons through several channels. Smuggling across the borders with Turkey, Iraq, Jordan and Lebanon is the main route, and Libya has been another source since its own arsenals were looted. Assault rifles, machine guns, anti-tank weapons and small arms move along these routes. Regional actors such as Iran and some Gulf states supply or broker arms, while factions also raid captured stores. The buying continues because local militias need guns to defend territory, press political demands and maintain leverage. Borders are hard to seal completely, and black markets keep functioning even when open aid or diplomacy shifts.

First off, 'all drugs are bad' is a bit of a shorthand. There are plenty of drugs that help. Antibiotics treat infection, insulin controls diabetes, and opioids can manage pain. None of that makes every chemical that enters the body bad. The issue is specific to reward, not chemistry in general. The real problem with the class of drugs you named is the reward signal itself. When a drug pushes the dopamine system hard, the brain treats it as an unusually valuable signal. Over time it compensates. That compensation is what produces tolerance and craving. You get less effect from the same dose, and the brain starts to expect the drug.

The drugs you named work on different receptors. Heroine is an opioid, it acts mainly on mu receptors. Coke stimulates dopamine and other monoamines. That mixture explains the mix of effects, from alertness to cardiac strain. A drug that gives intense pleasure but has zero adverse effects would have to be strong enough to trigger a big reward signal, but weak enough not to disturb anything else. That tension is the issue. Strong activation produces adaptation, and adaptation produces withdrawal symptoms when the drug is gone.

There is also a practical reason people chase the high. If pleasure is the goal, any side effects are often shrugged off at the time, then they become reasons for bigger doses. That is how escalation happens. You don't need a drug to have 'bad' side effects in the sense of toxicity. You just need the reward to be strong, the dose to be cheap and easy to get, and the body to adapt. Add easy access and you get the pattern.

A safer molecule can reduce some risks. Buprenorphine, for example, is an opioid that produces reward but has a ceiling effect that reduces the risk of overdose. It is not euphoric enough for many people looking for a strong high. Modafinil or caffeine can help with alertness with a modest reward component. None of them gives the intense euphoria people associate with heroin or cocaine without some cost. The cost is usually the body's attempt to keep homeostasis.

Those changes are the basis of tolerance and withdrawal. You can design a less harmful euphoriant, but zero adverse effects with intense pleasure is a hard ask because the same circuitry that creates the high is the circuitry that adapts and then misses the drug.

Hi Dave,

It’s probably a mix of sustained posture and dehydration, with stress layered in. Walking around for hours and carrying bags loads your back and legs. That’s only part of it. The crowds and bright lights add sensory load. The strain can tighten your neck and jaw, which is different from a normal headache but completely real.

Hydrate and stretch your calves and lower back. Take five minutes to sit down every 30 to 45 minutes. Don’t carry all the bags. Ask the shop for a trolley. If it gets sharp or one-sided, get it checked.

Alex

Hi Sam,

What your brother did is a very basic cognitive screen. Asking you to repeat silk five times checks attention and verbal repetition. Spelling it adds a motor speech component. The cow question checks simple semantic knowledge. Cows drink water, and milk is what cows produce. You likely answered milk because the association is so strong that it slips out before you can catch it. That can happen when you are tired, distracted, or a little off. If it happened once, don't read too much into it. If similar slips keep showing up, or if you notice word-finding or memory problems in daily life, ask for a proper cognitive evaluation. It's not proof of anything serious on its own. If he used a standard screening tool, ask which one. You can also ask him what exactly the test was meant to check and whether any scores were recorded.

Take care,
You

Hi Sam,

Start with the lender. A preapproval gives you a number, and that number should drive what you look at. Don't spend on a home you can't finance.

Inspections are non-negotiable. Get the report before you waive anything. Read the contract carefully. Keep the financing and inspection contingencies in place. The appraisal protects you if the lender values the home below the agreed price.

Keep deposit money with the escrow or title company, not the seller. Check the title report for liens or easements. If it's a condo, read the HOA budget and reserve study.

Compare at least three lenders. The rate matters, but points and closing costs can flip the total cost. Also check for prepayment penalties. Make your offer contingent on financing and inspection. Get every repair and credit in writing. If the seller won't agree to repairs, you can ask for a price credit or walk away.

Skip the 3-in-1 home warranty if you can afford the repairs yourself. For an older house, budget for major systems. HVAC, plumbing, roof, and electrical should be checked before closing.

Write to me if you want a second look at an offer or loan quote.

Best,
Alex

Hi Sam,

The main difference is formulation. A 3-in-1 product has to carry bodywash, shampoo and conditioner in one bottle, so the surfactants have to work at several pH levels and on different tissues. That means milder cleansing agents, more conditioning agents and added moisturizers. A 2-in-1 only has to balance cleansing and conditioning for hair. Single-purpose products can be much stronger in their one function.

In practice, the 3-in-1 is built for convenience, not maximum performance on any one job. It cleans skin and hair adequately and leaves some conditioning, but it won’t match a dedicated shampoo or a dedicated conditioner. If hair is short and you don’t mind a compromise, it’s fine. For long, damaged or heavily styled hair, a separate conditioner usually does better.

Also check the label for “sulfate-free” or “paraben-free” if that matters to you. Those affect how harsh the formula feels.

Best,
Alex

Hi Sam,

They don't put a speedometer on the crust. Plate motion is measured from position changes over time. The main tool is GPS. Ground stations record positions, and those positions are tracked over months and years. If a station moves 8 cm east in a year, that is a velocity of 8 cm/year. Velocities are modeled against a reference frame. GPS gives raw positions, then least-squares estimates position and rate for each station.

For longer records, we combine GPS with satellite radar. InSAR can resolve small displacements over months. VLBI and DSN are used for long baselines and for calibrating the frames. The reference frame matters. A station can look fast in one frame and slow in another, depending on which plate you subtract.

Most continental plates move between 1 and 10 cm per year, so you will not see the motion with the naked eye. In practice, agencies publish plate velocities. USGS has a Plate Motion Tool that uses GPS and plate model data. Check the ITRF version before comparing numbers. Then compare a station's mm/year value to the plate model. If you're tracking your own backyard, a consumer GPS won't give clean plate velocities.

Cheers,
Alex

Inbreeding raises the chance that a child receives the same variant from both parents. Most cognitive ability is polygenic, meaning many genes contribute small effects, and many harmful recessive variants sit hidden in healthy carriers. When relatives have children, shared ancestry makes matching variants more likely to become homozygous. The child can then express recessive mutations that would otherwise stay silent. This happens across many loci, so the effects add up. It is not one inbreeding gene. It is increased homozygosity plus accumulated small unfavorable effects.

The result is a population-level drop in average IQ, not a guarantee for every child. The science is simple Mendelian inheritance applied to many genes, not a single cause. In practice, close relatives share more DNA, so offspring are more likely to inherit two copies of rare alleles that lower cognitive scores. Breeders and geneticists track this with inbreeding coefficients. For humans, the effect is usually modest but measurable in population studies.

Your arm has more padding than many body regions. Muscle and fat sit between skin and bone, so a blow, shot, or stab is often absorbed in muscle before reaching bone or nerves. That is why an arm injury can seem milder than a similar injury to the ribs, abdomen, or head.

The arm is also farther from your spine and major organs. Most injuries land in muscle rather than in a nerve or vital structure. Wounds near a major nerve can hurt a lot, but the arm offers more buffer and fewer vital targets.

You also use your arm daily. Because you keep working, the brain tends to downplay the pain. Pain is a signal, not a fixed measurement. Arms do not have fewer pain receptors. The tissue layers, distance from central organs, and everyday use often make arm injuries feel less severe than injuries elsewhere for most people.

Carbon monoxide is dangerous because of what it does to the blood. CO binds hemoglobin about 200 times tighter than oxygen does. Once it latches on, that hemoglobin cannot carry oxygen, and the oxygen still bound to the remaining hemoglobin holds on too tightly and does not release where the tissues need it. It also shifts the oxygen-binding curve, making release harder at the cell level. The tissues get less oxygen than they need, even when the air still contains plenty of oxygen and the lungs are working normally. CO is also colorless and odorless, so people often don't notice it until the headache or dizziness sets in. The body makes small amounts of CO on its own, so a little is normal, but the CO you breathe in adds to that background level.

Carbon dioxide is the opposite situation. It is a normal waste product of metabolism, and the body is built to clear it. Most of the CO2 in the blood dissolves and converts to bicarbonate, and the lungs remove it on every exhale. At everyday levels, CO2 is routine chemistry the body runs all the time, so it is not inherently toxic. It becomes a problem only when it builds up, such as in a small sealed space, but that is a concentration issue, not something about the molecule itself. A room with many people and poor ventilation is the usual way CO2 gets high enough to matter. Breathing it at normal levels is just normal gas exchange, and the body handles the extra with each exhale.

That contrast is why CO is the poison: it directly cuts off oxygen delivery, while CO2 is a byproduct the body constantly clears. Put plainly, CO takes the oxygen slot and refuses to let go.

When an aircraft stops suddenly, your body keeps moving forward because of inertia. The brace position limits that forward movement. You bend your knees, grip your legs, and tuck your head toward your knees. This lowers your center of mass. The legs absorb the impact, not the spine or chest.

The main protective effect is that it keeps your head from striking the floor or other hard surfaces. It also helps you hold your breath and bite down on your tongue, which reduces the chance of swallowing during the jolt. In a crash, the legs take the load, and the lower posture protects the head and neck.

For a new colleague, the point is simple. The brace position turns a sudden stop from a whole-body problem into a problem your knees and shins can handle. It is the standard response taught in crew safety procedures for hard landings and crashes. The position also helps you stay in contact with the seat or floor, reducing the distance your body can travel before the stop is over. Hold it low, keep the head tucked, and let the legs do the work.

Most pre-industrial businesses were small and local. They were often tied to a family or a ruler. That structure kept them region-bound. They sold what nearby people needed, so their names rarely spread or survived. Industrialization changed that. Factories and railways let companies sell branded products across wider markets. Today's well-known companies mostly date from the industrial period and after. Many pre-industrial enterprises existed, but their limited scale and local records meant few became widely known. Company identity then depended on personal reputation, not logos or national supply chains. This is the practical reason the old business names are scarce.

I got the same pitch twice last month. "Only 3.99% for 60 days!" and I nearly fell for it, because the dealer's rate looked like a steal on paper. It's a teaser, not the real deal. Those low rates are usually good for a few payments, then the loan reprices to a higher number for the rest of the term, and you end up paying that higher rate on the balance for most of the loan.

I went with my bank instead. Same car, same price, and the bank's rate was a bit higher on the surface, but the total cost came out lower. What I actually compared: the dealer quoted a 4% teaser for 60 days, then 6.5% for the remaining 72 months, plus a 4% dealer-carry fee on the financed amount and a mandatory service package I didn't want. The bank quoted 5.5% flat for a 60-month term. When I ran the math, the bank's total interest was lower by a few thousand dollars, and I kept the car out of the dealer's hands for add-ons. I also dropped the extended warranty the finance guy kept trying to attach.

A few things to check before you sign. Ask the dealer to show the full amortization with the teaser ending and the rate jump. Look for the carry fee, which is usually a percentage of the loan and gets buried in the paperwork. And the term: dealers love 72-84 month loans because the monthly payment looks small and you sign up for years of interest. I'd take a shorter term and a slightly higher rate over a long cheap-looking one.

One more thing. The low rate is often limited to a promo model or a minimum down payment, so if your credit isn't perfect the teaser may not apply and the dealer will quote you the standard rate. The bank doesn't care which car you're buying, so you can set the term and pay schedule yourself, and I set mine to 60 months instead of 72.

So the "lower interest rate" is the headline, not the whole bill. Fees and term length are what actually decide the cost. I saved about 2,400 on the interest, and I'm not paying for a service package or a warranty I never asked for. Get the dealer to put the full amortization in writing before you sign. That single document kills most of the tricks.

The legality of marijuana in US states is a patchwork, and I think that’s fine. I’m for letting each state set its own rules, with one floor: a simple adult-use license and a fair tax. In Colorado, adult-use sales carry a 15% state excise, and local governments can add a 10% option tax. That revenue funds things like first-responder equipment and drug-diversion programs. New York’s law is stricter; it requires licensed retail stores, background checks, and 21+ purchase. I don’t think the federal government should rush to change the federal schedule. Several states have legalized recreational use, while still more allow medical use. The practical effect is that my friend in Oregon can buy a joint, my cousin in Florida can only use medical cannabis under a doctor’s certification, and I keep the two regimes separate. I want the federal baseline to stay light: a 21+ limit, a basic tax, and clear licensing.

I keep saying the body runs on electricity, but I mean a tiny version. I find the scale hard to picture. A neuron at rest sits around -70 millivolts across its membrane. The sodium-potassium pump shoves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in, burning ATP to keep that gradient. When a nerve fires, sodium channels open, sodium floods in, and the inside jumps toward +30 millivolts. Potassium then leaves, pulling it back down. That spike is the signal. No batteries, no wires. Just ion movement and membrane voltage.

I think most people picture sampling as cutting a snippet and dropping it into a new beat, but that undersells the actual work. The interesting part is what happens after you find the record. You rip the vinyl, load the slice into a sampler or DAW, and start editing. You’ll often have to match the sample’s tempo to your track. If the source is 90 BPM and your song is 120, you time-stretch or pitch-shift the clip, which changes the character of the sound. A vocal sample that was a warm soul chorus becomes a bright, metallic stab once you lift it a fifth. That transformation is the whole point. You’re not just quoting a song. You’re taking one fragment and making it feel like it was always part of the new piece.

The practical side involves a lot of digging. Musicians spend hours in record stores or through online crates, listening for that two-bar phrase with the right feel. Once you have it, you process it. A lowpass filter can strip the highs so a drum break sits under the kick. Reversing a vocal tail makes it sound alien and modern. Layering two samples, one pitched up and one down, thickens the texture. You might also chop the slice into 16th notes and reorder the hits on a step sequencer, or add a short delay to make it sit in the mix. It’s editing craft, not theft.

Then there’s the legal side, which is where sampling gets complicated. A short clip is not automatically free to use. The 1991 Bridgeport ruling established that even a two-second a cappella from a famous song can be infringement. For commercial releases you need to clear the sample with both the publisher, who owns the composition, and the label, who owns the master recording. That can mean paying a licensing fee or a share of royalties, and the paperwork takes time. Independent producers often skip that step, which is a gamble, but it’s a common practice in the underground.

My position is that sampling is a way of building music from the past. The old recording becomes raw material, and the producer’s skill is in choosing and reshaping that material. A sample only works when it disappears into the new song rather than standing out as a quotation. That’s where the real craft is.

My headache doesn't feel like my whole brain is swollen. I've learned to stop treating it that way. What hurts is the soft tissue around the brain: the meninges, scalp, and blood vessels. The brain itself doesn't have pain receptors. In my case, the pain usually tracks the trigeminal nerve, which branches across the forehead, temples, and behind the eyes. When a headache starts, I often get pressure and throbbing near the temples. If it's a tension type, I feel the scalp muscles pulled tight. The real trigger in my life is usually poor sleep, screen time, or missing meals. I've found that naming the type helps: vascular throbbing versus muscle tightness. That distinction matters because the remedies differ. I stop work, hydrate, use a cold pack, and take the appropriate medication. The headache stops when the nerve irritation settles, not because the brain "calms down."

We never got to eat, so I can't say if the food is good. We arrived at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday. We picked this spot because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel, thinking it would be easy. We put our names on their digital waitlist, which is useless. They told us to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We did, but we stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually mentioned we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15 p.m. It was just a party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait extends that far past payment, tell people upfront so our night isn't completely wasted. Absolute disaster. Zero stars if that were an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and surprisingly, there was no line at all. For two people, the bill came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I had expected to pay at one.

I was disappointed that steak wasn’t offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things I feel like you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was that there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any.

Overall, I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

Four stars. I'm keeping it. The space bar rattles; hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so "example" becomes "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking. I paid $38 and kept it anyway because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison. My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle. Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I've been going to Vegas for pretty much my whole life. I mean the under 21 version of it. I've sat through lots of shows before I was old enough to gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught. I'd call it mixed, maybe a bit worse than mixed.

The circular stage is the smart part. You look down into it, so from almost any seat you get a decent view. That's rare in Vegas. A few acts are impressive. The strength work, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are real athletes, no question. It also reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not exactly a rip-off, just that if you've seen Cirque, you've seen similar feats, probably with more clarity.

Clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don't know. Maybe there's a dream, maybe a guy, maybe water. It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never says what it's trying to say. Also, too much is happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments stacked together. A more restrained production would hit harder. It has that stereotypical Vegas spectacle feel, as if more must be better, so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you're staying at the Wynn or Encore, there's a deal. You can get it for $99 instead of the usual $125. That helps. Would I go back? Probably not. I wouldn't pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn't blown away, and I don't think anyone else was either. A few friends did like it. If you haven't seen it, maybe check it out. Just don't expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago we ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear by telephone. The sales rep wrote down the delivery address wrong: her handwritten 7 was read as a 1. We meant 5407, but the shirts went to 5401. The people at 5401 took the package to the local UPS store to have it returned, then it just disappeared and we did not find out for weeks. While that dispute was going on, we ordered two more shirts. Rockmount would not refund the first two. At that stage, the owner took over. He admitted the shipment had gone to the wrong address but said no refund until the shirts were sent back. He also said it was partly on us because we had not been friendly enough to the neighbors at 5401, four doors down. We disputed the original charge with our credit card company, and we eventually received a credit we had requested from them.
